items.title: Dr Reddy's receives DCGI approval for esophageal cancer drug Zytorvi
items.summary:
Dr Reddy's Laboratories on Wednesday said it has received approval from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) for Zytorvi (toripalimab), through which it aims to expand access to first-line immunotherapy for patients with advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) in India.
The drug has been approved in combination with cisplatin and paclitaxel for the first-line treatment of adult patients with unresectable advanced, recurrent, or metastatic ESCC, the pharma company said in a release.
This marks Zytorvi's second approved indication in the country, expanding beyond nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
ESCC accounts for approximately 80 per cent of all esophageal cancer cases in India, the company said.
Zytorvi contains toripalimab, a monoclonal antibody that binds to PD-1 and blocks its interaction with PD-L1 and PD-L2, thereby supporting T-cell activity against cancer cells.

items.title: Asian Para Games 2026: Sachin Khilari leads India's shot put medal sweep
items.summary:
Sachin Sarjerao Khilari won a gold with a Games record as Indians swept all three medals in the men's shot put F46 event at the Asian Para Games here on Wednesday.
Paris Paralympics silver winner Khilari defended the gold he had won in the previous Asian Para Games in China with his sixth and final throw of 15.87m, breaking the earlier Games record of 15.67m.
Mohd. Yasser took the silver with his third round throw of 15.06m while Parveen was third with 14.94m.
The F46 classification is for field athletes with a single above or below elbow amputation, or an equivalent upper-limb impairment. They compete in a standing position and generate throwing power using their hips and legs.

Besides, the rupee got a boost from the foreign dollar inflows tied to the Jio IPO, which opened for public subscription on Wednesday, according to analysts.
However, elevated crude oil prices and a firm US dollar capped the gains.
At the interbank foreign exchange market, the rupee opened stronger at  94.78, and then gained further ground to touch 94.62 against the American currency, registering a gain of 29 paise from its previous close.
On Monday, the rupee settled lower by 2 paise at 94.91 against the US dollar.
The forex market was closed on Tuesday on account of Dussehra.

items.title: France has a proud tradition of protesting
items.summary: PARIS - No nation does mass protests quite like France.When the French fight high fuel taxes, they don yellow vests and march. When angry farmers want better pay, hundreds of them drive tractors down the Champs-Elysees. And when museum workers want better tourist management, they strike and shut down the Louvre.Passionate public protest is as French as "La Marseillaise," the 1792 anthem that enshrines the collective duty to fight tyranny in the country's national identity. But this month, the most violent demonstrations in years - and tough policing - have raised concern about riots overshadowing hundreds of thousands of peaceful demonstrators marching against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.Also read: France unrest leaves global brands with a burning problemOn Saturday alone, at least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings, looted stores and engulfed a historic city hall in flames. More protests could be in store."How can French people do this to France?" outgoing President Emmanuel Macron asked on Sunday. Nothing justifies the destruction, he added. "We all feel anger and shame."But any student of French history would know that the nation's proud, loud and colorful protest culture has sometimes turned violent - starting with the beheadings of King Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette during the revolution that overthrew the monarchy in 1789.A protest culture is bornHistorians say the revolution was where the modern-day French tradition of civic engagement as a duty was born. The idea is that voting is not the only way to drive change; demonstration is considered a bedrock value, a way to make elites hear the populace and to defend freedoms. The moment a child becomes an activist is seen as a generations-old rite of passage. The right to protest is even constitutionally protected."It's a way to build collective identity and political community," said Magali Della Sudda, research director in political science at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Bordeaux.France's post-revolution history is not a solid story of protests and reforms, but of cycles of popular uprisings, repression, mobilization and political concessions. The tradition has turned tragic; In 1871, government troops cracked down on the new "Paris Commune," or municipal government, reportedly killing thousands.In some ways, collective action won - as in 1968, when student demonstrations and a general strike forced the government to grant concessions like an increase in the minimum wage.In more recent history, the "yellow vests" - "gilets jaunes" in French - demonstrated against a proposed fuel tax increase, and that broadened into protests over other issues like living costs and inequality. Some demonstrations in 2018 and 2019 featured burning cars, looting and confrontations with police. It's not uncommon for French violence on the fringes to mar otherwise peaceful marches.Likewise, the student protests over the weekend expanded from education to other grievances - and featured dramatic scenes of looting and clashes with police. It's not clear how many of those who were ransacking shops had turned out to join the day's protest, which drew tens of thousands, or were mere opportunists. Authorities have responded with nightly curfews; there were calls for more protests later in the week.Also read: With France embroiled in protest, a look at the nation's economic standing by the numbersPolice violence blamed for mistrustSome of the forces driving protests for the last month owe to more recent French tradition, according to political scientist Fabien Jobard, who has studied the history of protest and policing.Since the 1990s, the country has seen recurring waves of what the French call "violences urbaines" and Americans would call riots, Jobard said. They are often sparked by police violence: nationwide unrest erupted in 2005 after two teenagers died while fleeing police, and again in 2023 after an officer fatally shot a 17-year-old during a traffic stop outside Paris."For young people from the suburbs, the riot is one of the traditional forms of collective expression," he said.Government critics and human rights campaigners have alleged that police tactics in the last month have been unnecessarily violent. Much of the criticism focuses on rubber-bullet launchers, known in France as LBDs, and stun grenades, which critics blame for serious injuries to protesters.And Della Sudda noted that the nearly 8,000 arrests in the weeks leading up to Oct. 17 dwarf the few dozen detained during a 1998 protest of 500,000 students against teacher shortages and dilapidated schools.The feeling of not being heard also is part of it, she says. Rather than listen to protesters and negotiate, Della Sudda noted for example, the government tried to appease "yellow vest" grievances through a digital platform, which translates to "the great national debate." Anti-government protesters panned Macron's plan."As a result," Della Sudda wrote, "mistrust is growing."

items.title: China opposes US sanctions on five firms linked to ex-Google engineer
items.summary:
Beijing on Tuesday expressed "firm opposition" to the Trump administration's sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to a former Google engineer accused of intellectual property theft.
The move "severely harms the legitimate rights and interests" of Chinese businesses, the country's commerce ministry said in a statement. "The nature of this act is egregious. China firms opposes this."
The ministry also urged the US to "correct its erroneous practice" and said Beijing would take "necessary measures", without specifying them.
It came a day after the US State Department imposed sanctions on five Chinese companies connected to Linwei Ding, who founded Shanghai Zhisuan Technology. The department said he had touted his experience with Google and claimed his company could replicate the American tech giant's super intelligence infrastructure technology.

items.title: Delhi Police transfers second case against CJP leaders' to Crime Branch
items.summary:
Delhi Police on Tuesday transferred another case registered against Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to the Crime Branch, sources said.
The Crime Branch will now investigate two cases against the CJP leaders. The other case linked to Das and Ranka allegedly entering the Jantar Mantar area was transferred to the Crime Branch on Monday.
According to Delhi Police, on October 13, Das, Ranka, Ajinkya Shinde and 11 other members of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) reached Jantar Mantar, which has been denotified as a designated protest site, by trespassing through private premises.
Police personnel deployed at the spot intervened and tried to stop them. All 14 people were detained and two FIRs were registered.
Das and Ranka were sent to five-day judicial custody on October 14 by a Special Executive Magistrate for breaching peace bonds. Their judicial custody was extended by two days on Monday.

The next edition of the Quad Summit is set to be held on the margins of the ASEAN Summit in the Philippines next month, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, US President Donald Trump and leaders of Australia and Japan are expected to attend the summit during the ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) Summit scheduled for November 16 to 17 in Manila.
In an interview, the US Secretary of State told Network 18 that the US hoped the Quad Summit would be held before year-end.
"We are going to do it in Manila, at the ASEAN conference. We don't have the specific date yet, but that's going to happen, and we're very enthusiastic about it," he said.
"We look forward to being a part of that at ASEAN here in just a few weeks," Rubio added.
India had planned to host the Quad Leaders' Summit last year, but it did not take place as there was no clarity from Washington on Trump's visit to the country.

items.title: Philanthropy’s biggest failure is its fear of failure
As slow as an India-US trade deal
items.summary: There are forces who have probably been assigned the task of ensuring that Marco Rubio doesn't overhear this during the next few days he's here in India. But India is a big and loud place, and this corner column only mirrors it. So, consider our duty to put on record a new idiomatic phrase in English that has gained traction over the last few months: 'As slow as an India-US trade deal'.Those familiar with formulations such as 'watching paint dry' and 'waiting for Godot' may already know what we're talking about. Except, this latest idiom describes an activity that is simultaneously happening, not happening, and about to happen.Its most remarkable feature is its elasticity. A delayed flight is merely late. A delayed marriage may be called off. But something proceeding 'as slow as an India-US trade deal' enjoys permanent forward momentum without the inconvenience of arriving.Whenever an official announces that negotiations are 'almost complete', seasoned observers understand that it's nudge-nudge, wink-wink for another postponement. 'We are very close' means further away than previously feared. 'Final stages' suggests the beginning of another round. 'Constructive discussions' indicates that nobody has thrown a chair. Trade negotiators on both sides of the Indo-Pacific water table have finally produced something of lasting value: a phrase.

items.title: France: Curfews bring calm to Paris
items.summary: PARIS: Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend marred by France's most destructive rioting in years, as authorities imposed curfews in several cities in an effort to prevent another round of rioting and looting.At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings and engulfed a historic city hall in flames, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.Also Read: Paris police issue overnight curfew in 2 areas of French capital to try to prevent further disorderIn the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. on Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter circled over Place de la Republique overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the order was being respected.Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, a reference to the " yellow vest " protests over fuel prices that began in 2018 and shook the first term of President Emmanuel Macron.Workers then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument."The targeted curfews helped keep last night calm," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Tuesday, adding that new curfews would be imposed that night "wherever the situation requires," decided locally by prefects, the state's representatives in each region, together with mayors.Speaking in Lille, northern France, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,500 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and imprisoned immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.The National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yael Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."

items.title: Giant 'heat storms' are scorching the Earth
items.summary: By Maurice Tamman, Ben Welsh, Pete Mckenzie, Charlie Szymanski, Delgerzaya Delgerjargal, Robbie Corey-Boulet, Loucoumane Coulibaly, Jeff Horwitz and Joan FausIn less than a lifetime, about six and a half decades, heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time.The largest heat wave of the 1960s reached about 6% of the planet as it drifted for 46 days over the Atlantic Ocean, parts of Latin America and West Africa.The largest one this decade swept across almost 85% of the globe during its 367-day lifetime, stretching into the polar latitudes and touching virtually every human being on Earth.To continue calling such sprawling phenomena "heat waves" would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen meteorologists and climate researchers - and analyzed temperatures for every hour of every day since 1960 for more than one million grid squares covering the entire globe. Out of those results we developed a new concept: the "heat storm."Simply put, heat storms are supersized heat waves. Reuters uses a conservative benchmark to define an ordinary heat wave: five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures. Then we define the largest heat waves - those that at their peak cover at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada - as heat storms.Applying this definition, Reuters identified a startling transformation. Heat storms were rare in the 1960s, when they averaged about five active storms per year. This decade, heat storms have swarmed the planet, averaging about 102 a year.One of them caused this summer's deadly heat in Europe, notching the highest June temperatures ever recorded in Bordeaux, Budapest, and Bilbao, the latter of which hit 42.7 degrees Celsius (108.9 degrees Fahrenheit). Roasting Europe for most of June and July, the heat storm warped steel railroad tracks, drove what European governments estimated were more than 10,000 excess deaths in a single week, and prompted Belgian zookeepers to cool their tigers by feeding them raw meat encased in ice.The largest heat storm on record - the one that lasted for 367 days over 2023-2024 and reached almost 85% of the globe - sent temperatures in parts of the Philippines up to 38 C (100.5 F), immiserating students in the country's mostly unairconditioned schools. In Manila, math teacher Joel Arrojado recalled a student who was face-down at his desk, crying. When Arrojado coaxed the boy into looking up, Arrojado saw his face and chest covered in blood. The boy, Arrojado said, had suffered a spontaneous nosebleed, a common problem in extreme heat. As more blood pumped from his nostrils, Arrojado recalled, the child pleaded with Arrojado to call his mother.As the same heat storm encased southern Louisiana for months, it exacerbated a historic drought.The state burned, suffering what the governor called "theworst wildfire we've seen since at least the Second World War" - and close to 600 other fires in August alone. Two months later, smoke from a smoldering marsh fire developed into a blinding "super fog" that caused a highway pile-up of at least 158 cars, killing seven people.The same heat storm helped fuel a 2023 Mediterranean cyclone that dropped massive rains over Libya. In the dead of night, two dams burst near the coastal town of Derna, washing away entire neighborhoods. A week later, on her hands and knees, Sabreen Blil clawed with her bare hands at the rubble of her brother's house, hoping to dig out the dead. As she wept, she recited their names. "Taym, Yazan, Luqman, Salmah, Tumador, Hakim and his wife. Oh my God. My family, where are you?" she wailed. "Oh God. Even just one - my God - just let me find even one body."During the annual Hajj pilgrimage in Saudi Arabia, the heat storm drove temperatures at Mecca's Grand Mosque to 51.8 C (125.2 F), killing more than 1,300 pilgrims. Bodies lay in the streets. And as Europe's largest recorded fire spread in Greece during the span of that same heat storm, the inferno killed migrants traversing the thick Dadia forest. Their corpses remained in the woods for days; even the vultures that might have fed on the bodies had fled the flames.These far-flung and seemingly unrelated catastrophes all shared a common connection: one single heat storm.Heat storms inflict "a major disruption to global civilization," said James Renwick, professor of physical geography at New Zealand's Victoria University of Wellington. "Heat is the biggest killer from climate change," he said, noting that it can lead to "famine, hunger, death, conflict over resources."A NEW WAY TO UNDERSTAND CLIMATE CHANGEHeat storms constitute a new way to conceptualize how Earth's climate is changing as humanity pumps greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.The determination by climatologists that the average global temperature in 2025 was 1.47 C (2.6 F) above the pre-industrial level is useful to scientists and policymakers, but to many people it's so abstract as to be meaningless. What people do understand are heat waves - in Spanish, an "ola de calor"; in Arabic, a "mawjat hararia"; in Mandarin, a "re lang."Yet no universal definition of a heat wave exists. For example, authorities differ over duration: The US National Weather Service defines a heat wave as "abnormally and uncomfortably hot" weather typically lasting "two or more days," while the meteorological agencies of Australia, France, Spain and the United Kingdom set the threshold at three days. Some of those countries also have different rules for what temperatures qualify as a heat wave.Moreover, what constitutes a heat wave in Anchorage, Alaska, would not be considered a heat wave in Kuwait City. The climate in those places differs sharply, and a heat wave is an unusual period of hot weather for a particular place.Such dueling definitions made it all but impossible to gauge whether heat waves are more common globally now than in the past. But the system Reuters has devised delivers the precision needed to do so.We began by determining the historical temperature range for each day of the year from 1961 to 1990 for each of 1.04 million grid squares around the globe. The temperature data comes from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and our detailed methodology is here. A heat wave occurs when the daily high temperature for any location reaches at least the 90th percentile of the historical range - in other words, the hottest 10% - for five days in a row.So a July heat wave in Istanbul is five or more consecutive days of at least 25.6 C (78.1 F), whereas one in Phoenix, Arizona, needs to reach 40.3 C (104.5 F).In Reuters' definition, a heat wave can happen in any season, so in Istanbul a January heat wave would be five consecutive days of at least (11.2 C) (52.2 F), and in Phoenix the threshold would be 20.8 C (69.4 F).To measure the geographical extent of heat waves, we map neighboring heat wave grid squares that form a cohesive area. Because very large heat waves exert an expanding effect on the planet's rising temperatures, Reuters created a further definition: If at any point a heat wave covers 1% of the planet, we designate it a heat storm and give it a name, as is done with tropical storms and hurricanes.Naming events is "a powerful way for people to understand that something is happening," Anthony Leiserowitz, director of the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication, told Reuters. Yet "we don't currently do that with heat waves," he said, even though heat has been estimated to kill almost half a million people a year. Defining and naming heat storms is an important innovation, he added, and could help people to track impacts and consequences.As their numbers have swelled over the decades, heat storms and heat waves have not only caused individual catastrophes. They have also helped drive lasting, systemic effects.They exacerbate droughts and intensify fires - from Chile to Europe, the largest conflagrations on record happened during heat storms - and if they hit while a woman is pregnant, studies have found that she's more likely to suffer everything from stillbirth to preeclampsia, a leading killer of expecting and post-partum women.Warmer temperatures can usher in benefits, at least for some regions. Siberia now produces almost as much wheat as Russia's traditional breadbasket near the Black Sea. That's in part because increasing heat storms and heat waves have helped open far northern latitudes to agriculture while simultaneously contributing to droughts around the Black Sea that reduce production there.18 YEARS OF CONSTANT HEAT STORMSTens of thousands of ordinary heat waves flicker in and out of existence every year. Like heat storms, they too have escalated in number, more than doubling from the 1960s to this decade. The vast majority are small, however, never even covering 0.01% of the planet, about the size of a square that you could drive across in less than two and a half hours. Only a minuscule fraction of heat waves ever gets big enough to become heat storms, which currently number about 102 annually.Yet heat storms now claim the lion's share of Earth's unusually hot days, those in the top tenth of the historical range. In the 1960s, heat storms averaged 3% a year for any given spot on the planet. (The remainder comprised ordinary heatwaves and short bursts of heat that didn't last long enough to become a heatwave.)This decade, heat storms have accounted for almost 43% of such days.As greenhouse gas emissions have increased, so too have heat storms and ordinary heat waves. From the 1960s to this decade, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by more than 30%. Over that time, the average portion of the planet likely to be covered by heat storms and heat waves has risen more than 12-fold. El Nino - the periodic episodes of unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean that drive major weather patterns - has acted as an accelerant, intensifying heat storms and heat waves.Reuters has also examined the opposite of heat waves and heat storms - cold snaps and cold storms. They have dwindled. From the 1960s to this decade, the total area in a cold snap or cold storm on an average winter day has shrunk by almost 80%.Despite their mammoth scale, the phenomenon of heat storms has been largely invisible to the public. Until recent decades, heat storms were rarer and smaller, so easier to overlook.But perhaps as importantly, they hadn't been defined and named in the sharp way that typhoons and hurricanes are. Yes, people in Montreal, Perth and Hong Kong knew they were baking in a stretch of hot days - but they did not know that they were all experiencing one unitary heat storm.As part of this series examining heat storms and their effects, Reuters has integrated an online Heat Storm Tracker into our regular weather coverage. With this tool, people can see what had previously gone unnoticed and, using that knowledge, tally the impact of heat storms as they rage across regions.The rapid evolution of heat has not only made individual heat storms larger. Now, in sharp contrast to even 20 years ago, massive heat storms often run into, merge with, and split off from one another. What has become common are heat storms that run consecutively, simultaneously or both - heat storm cascades.The duration of these cascades swelled from an average of roughly two months in the 1960s to nine months in the first part of the 2000s. Then, on July 6, 2008, a cascade started - and has not stopped. For more than 18 years straight, 6,681 days, at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one.Many of them have been colossal. In the almost half century between 1960 and the start of the current 18-year cascade, only five heat storms had ever reached a peak size bigger than a tenth of the planet, about the area of Europe and Asia combined. The ongoing cascade has included 56 such mega heat storms.The largest of these was one we have named Heat Storm Vera, the storm that killed the Hajj pilgrims, intensified the Louisiana wildfires, and touched nearly 85% of the planet over its 367-day lifespan.What follows is a biography of Vera, from its birth on July 29, 2023, through its last day on July 29, 2024, that shows how the storm connected and often devastated communities scattered across the globe.TEXAS, AUGUST 2023: FRIDAY NIGHT LIGHTSOn a sweltering evening in August 2023, as Heat Storm Vera coiled around the American South, Justice Trumpler led his high school football team onto the field for the season's first game. In hopes of playing college ball, the 17-year-old captain had invited coaches and recruiters to watch. As the game kicked off at 7:30pm, the temperature was 37.8 C (100 F).Texas's passion for high school football - the American version, not the one that transfixed billions during this summer's World Cup - was captured in the iconic movie Friday Night Lights, about a team gunning for the state championship. But players of American football suffer 11 times as many heat-related injuries as athletes in all other sports combined, according to data from the University of Connecticut Korey Stringer Institute.That's because the football season starts in the summer, the sport demands intense physical exertion, and many of its players, such as the 255-pound offensive lineman Trumpler, have large bodies that are harder to cool down. There's another reason: In contrast to most other warm-weather sports, American football features heat-trapping helmets and heavy padding.Meanwhile, Texas is spending ever more time in extreme heat. Across the entire three decades from 1960 to 1989, the city of Austin - home to Trumpler's Bowie High School - experienced a total of 557 days in heat waves and heat storms. This decade, our analysis shows, that number has already surpassed 700. During the football season, Heat Storm Vera enveloped Austin for 39 days.By halftime, the Bowie Bulldogs led 14-0. As the teams broke apart, Trumpler's parents said they watched him walk to the field's edge and vomit. A trainer hosed it away.Through the second half, they saw Trumpler stop to dry heave at least twice, they said, and he seemed slow to get off the turf after plays. At one point, his parents saw him walk toward the opposing team's huddle, a sign of mental confusion.Trumpler's father, Jason Trumpler, told Reuters he began shouting from the bleachers for the coaches to pull his son out of the game. When that didn't work, he went to the railing separating the stands from the field and continued yelling. Trumpler kept playing.Bowie's coach did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The school's principal referred Reuters to a school district spokesman, who did not respond to messages seeking comment.Other players struggled, too. So many boys fell to the ground after plays that Bowie's game commentators declared it a "cramp epidemic." By the fourth quarter, the score was tied. The coaches could have ended the game, but the referee announced it would go into overtime."Both teams are going to start on the 25 (yard line) of their opposition and, uh, keep on going until somebody dies," said one commentator. "Don't say that," replied the other.The "unfortunate" phrasing, the first commentator told Reuters, was intended to convey how hard the teams were playing under very tough conditions.Just before the second-to-last play, a leg cramp brought Trumpler to the ground. His coach finally pulled him out. "Texas has that mentality of 'you gotta be tough, you gotta play through pain,'" said Jason.Jason took Trumpler home, but the teen couldn't stop throwing up. After an ice bath failed to cool Trumpler down, Jason said, he drove his son to the hospital. When Trumpler's mother, Jennifer Norman-Wolfe, arrived, he couldn't recognize her voice, she said, and couldn't tell her how many brothers he had.Reuters was not able to review Trumpler's medical records, but his parents said tests showed their son's kidneys were failing, and his brain was swelling so much that doctors said they might need to drill a hole in his skull to relieve the pressure. Doctors couldn't assure them their son would survive, they said.Twelve high school football players in the US have died from heat over the last decade, according to statistics compiled by the National Center for Catastrophic Sport Injury Research. Trumpler was released after two days in the hospital.Later, his parents said, they sent his medical records to Bowie High School and tried to discuss what had gone wrong. But they said the school's athletic staff infuriated them by suggesting they hadn't done enough to alert coaches about his condition during the game, Trumpler's father told Reuters. A month later, Trumpler's parents saw a video of an official for the governing body for Texas high school sports, the University Interscholastic League, referring to their son's injury as a "questionable" heat-related incident.Neither the school district nor the UIL official responded to requests for comment. In an interview, UIL Executive Director Jamey Harrison said that the organization relies on schools to report the details of medical events and avoids instituting rules based on individual incidents.Heat storms are starting to reshape Texas football. State filings show that since the beginning of this year, at least four school districts in the state have registered to build indoor or covered practice spaces, two with price tags in excess of $10 million. And this year, the UIL adopted new rules requiring rest breaks, ice baths and shortenings or cancellations of practices in high heat. Yet these rules are not mandatory for football games themselves.Two weeks after his hospitalization, as Heat Storm Vera continued baking Austin, Trumpler resumed playing football. He declined to speak to Reuters, but wrote on X at the time that "it felt so good to return."His heat injury, however, seemed to throw off college recruiters. Division I teams, those with the biggest and best programs, stopped calling, Trumpler's father recalled. His mother said Trumpler himself seemed tepid about the prospect, which had once been his dream, and he is not currently attending college."Our son, Justice, is tough and built for football, mentally and physically," she wrote at the time. "This heat was tougher."SPAIN, AUGUST 2023: "PIRATES OF LIQUID GOLD"Early in the morning of August 30, 2023, a team of thieves carefully maneuvered a tanker truck through the winding roads of the small Spanish town of Carcabuey, intent on an audacious heist.Around 2:30 a.m., according to a local police official, the thieves pulled into a gated driveway on the edge of town. They shut off lights and cut through the rickety gate's padlock. They left no fingerprints because they wore gloves. Once inside, they beelined for their unusual loot: extra virgin olive oil, which they siphoned from industrial-sized tanks.Over the previous several months, a series of heat storms had helped fuel a drought that devastated the olive crop and sent the price of olive oil skyrocketing, raising the value of the stolen 56 metric tons to a staggering $546,000. Journalists nicknamed the thieves the Pirates of Liquid Gold.By dawn, when the olive mill's manager, Martin Parras, arrived, all that remained was an oil streak on the driveway. Parras was so overcome, he said, that he walked into a nearby olive grove, sat beneath the trees and wept.In Spain's southern region around Carcabuey, houses are painted white to repel the sun, and residents take long breaks during the hot afternoons. Olive trees, which evolved to have formidable heat tolerance, have thrived here for centuries.But the trees have struggled in the new heat storm era. Between March 12 and August 1, when Vera first reached Carcabuey, the little town endured eight other heat storms that rolled one into the next with almost no break. The combination of early heat and scarce rain burned the olive flowers, preventing them from opening and pollinating, Parras said.In the past five to 10 years, locals say, the heat that once lasted from June to August can now stretch from April to November, and it stays hot later into the evening. "People used to go out around 7 or 8 in summers but now it can be 9 or 9:30 and there's no one in the streets," said Juan Lara, who has been running a pastry shop near Carcabuey for 46 years.Heat Storm Vera spent a total of 127 days over Carcabuey. At first, Vera teased the city, brushing it briefly before smothering the town for three weeks until a couple of days before the theft. Temperatures surpassed 40 C (104 F) several times.Parras said about half the olives at his Marin Serrano El Lagar mill ended up unusable, with scant flesh and barely any oil. "Olive trees had a yellow color like when grass dries, and leaves fell," he recalled. "It was monstrous."The price of olive oil spiked by 44% that year, largely because the withering heat and drought reduced output by roughly half in Spain, the world's largest producer. Some Spanish supermarkets placed alarms on bottles to prevent theft, but no one thought thieves would target a mill's huge metal tanks. At Marin Serrano El Lagar, the only alarms were in the office and a room storing oil that was already bottled.Spanish police arrested a 50-year-old man who had crushed olives at the mill for more than two decades until he left in 2020 after an argument over his salary. Authorities suspect the man conspired to steal the oil with the owner of a rival mill just down the road, the local police official said. The owner was also arrested. Both men were later released, but remain under investigation. They told Reuters they did not steal the oil, with the 50-year-old suspect saying he's eager to clear his name.The real culprit, according to mill manager Parras, has not been indicted. "Climate change has completely affected olive fields," he said. "Has it been the cause of the theft? Totally." If the heat hadn't driven the price so high, he added, "There would have been no theft."BRAZIL, SEPTEMBER 2023: DEATH OF THE DOLPHINSOn September 28, 2023, an environmental scientist named Ayan Fleischmann sat in a small boat at the heart of a vast Amazonian lake and watched a dolphin die. The creature moved in jagged circles, its body shuddering. Suddenly, it sank.As Fleischmann watched the dolphin vanish into the darkness of Lake Tefe, smoke from nearby wildfires fouled the air. An algal bloom stained the waters blood-red. Dozens of dolphin corpses dotted the lake's beaches. Photos taken by Fleischmann's team show the dolphins' skin wrinkled like melted plastic or peeling to reveal yellow flesh. This, Fleischmann recalled thinking, might be what Hell looks like.With its distinctive pink color, the river dolphin is one of the Amazon's most iconic and mythologized creatures. According to legend, they would transform into humans at night to seduce locals. The dolphin was put on the endangered species list eight years ago, after poaching and rainforest destruction caused its numbers to plummet. Now, heat storms have emerged as an urgent new threat.Heat Storm Vera settled over the Amazon in late July and spent a total of nearly seven months over Lake Tefe, simmering it for 42 days in a row before Fleischmann watched the dolphin die. The heat storm helped warm the lake to a high of 41 C (105.8 F) - the temperature of a standard jacuzzi. For the dolphins, such temperatures were catastrophic: Fleischmann's research team later concluded that the creatures had effectively been cooked alive.Fleischmann, 34, had been studying how the waters of Lake Tefe were changing for several years. "It became a friend. I see it every day," he said. But as the heat storm festered, he recalled, so much of the lake dried up that when he and his colleagues visited local villages, they were pelted by whirlwinds of sand whipped up from newly exposed beaches.Later, Fleischmann's research institute autopsied the dolphins that washed up on the lake's shores. Temperatures were so high that most of the corpses rotted faster than they could be studied, said Hilda Chavez-Perez, a biologist who oversaw the study of the bodies. But in those they could examine, she said, the researchers kept finding that the dolphins' brains were bruised and their organs speckled with blood: telltale signs of heat stress. Many had empty stomachs, indicating that they had lost the ability to feed in the heat.The lake's normal population is at least 700 river dolphins, said Fleischmann, but during September and October, when Vera scalded the area for all but one day, more than 200 died. "Nobody had ever seen that magnitude of mortality," he said. "It was like a death circus."POLAND, FEBRUARY 2024: WEIRD WINTERSIn Poland's Tatra Mountains, the first months of 2024 were full of strange signs.In mid-February, bears woke from hibernation weeks early and began roaming the ranges. Frogs also emerged early, ranger Tomasz Zając remembered, rising from the rotting leaves and underwater silt beneath which they had hunkered through the cold months. Although snow still clung to the high peaks, it was so slushy that it frequently slipped in mini-avalanches that left black scars of exposed rock.While heat storms are hottest in summer, they can also mellow typically frigid months. Heat Storm Vera, which enveloped the Tatras for 31 days in January and February, sent the temperature up to 17 C (62.6 F). In neighboring Germany, Vera prompted the country's weather service to tell people to leave behind their warm coats as they celebrated the annual winter carnival, while in the UK, television hosts joked about unusually "hot and steamy" Valentine's Day temperatures in the English town of Lover.But winter heat storms can also cause unexpected harm. In January of this year, bone-chilling cold descended on eastern Canada and the US, causing Toronto to endure 23 straight days of sub-freezing cold and gripping parts of Minnesota in temperatures that plunged to minus 41.7 C (minus 43 F). Paradoxically, those frigid temperatures were largely caused by winter heat waves in the northern polar regions and Greenland, where residents basked in unseasonably balmy days that reached 11.3 C (52.3 F). That northern mass of warm air shunted a cold front down over eastern North America, in what climatologists call a polar vortex.Tennessee got so cold that freezing rain encased trees in ice, causing many to collapse under the weight. Forest silence was occasionally broken by a sound resembling gunshots as sap froze and expanded, splintering tree trunks. Almost half of Pittsburgh's snowplows stopped working, forcing the city to leave roads uncleared for days and trash on the streets for a week. The extreme cold killed at least 100 people across the US, caused power losses for more than a million customers, drove more flight cancellations than any time since the COVID 19 pandemic, and forced school closures from Milwaukee to Atlanta. Even in Cuba, farmers woke to frost on their crops.Heat Storm Vera spent weeks over Europe in January and February, effectively transforming winter into spring. By mid-February, local media estimated that a quarter of European ski resorts were closed due to lack of snow. It was so warm that many resorts couldn't even make artificial powder. Amid the unseasonal heat, intense rain battered parts of Europe and neighboring countries; as Vera settled over the southern Turkish city of Antalya, flash floods inundated entire neighborhoods, with the sudden flow submerging fire trucks and buses.In the Tatra Mountains, winter's end is marked by the blossoming of crocuses. More than a hundred million typically bloom starting in mid- to late-March, turning the valleys into purple oceans. Rangers have to patrol Chochołowska Glade - where crocuses bloom most densely - to prevent tourists stampeding the flowers into the ground. In late February, that frenzy was supposed to be weeks away. But on February 29, ranger Zając noticed a flash of color amidst Chochołowska's freshly-uncovered grass. He squatted to get a better look at the purple petals unfolding around an orange stamen. Earlier than he could ever remember, the first crocus had arrived.THE PHILIPPINES, APRIL 2024: COLLAPSING CHILDRENPartway through April 2024, on the top floor of Saghakan High School in the Philippines' Tacloban City, Jeffrey Polido was giving a lesson on typhoons to 50 sweating 14-year-olds in a concrete classroom with two rickety fans. Interrupting him, a student burst through the door with news: Yet another child had collapsed.Polido - a 37-year-old science teacher who at that time ran the school's health clinic - raced outside to the stricken girl and took her vitals. He and the student who had alerted him carried the child down several flights of stairs to the clinic to recover. Then, Polido walked back to his roasting classroom and resumed teaching, knowing it would happen all over again. After all, he told Reuters, he had already seen dozens of students collapse.Polido, along with the teacher who comforted the student with the gushing nosebleed, didn't know it but they were on the frontline of Heat Storm Vera. The heat was intensified by its most dangerous accomplice: humidity. As a result, a temperature of 33 C (91.4 F) in steamy Tacloban felt like 47 C (116.5 F), while hotter parts of the Philippines reached "feels like" levels of 53 C (127.5 F) - at which point the country's weather bureau warned, "Heat stroke is imminent." For the millions of children in schools cooled only by fans, the thick muggy heat was especially dangerous.In Manila, Jenita Simangan, 49, watched her 50-strong class of five-year-olds break out into rashes, complain of headaches, and say the heat made their skin feel like it was burning, she recalled. Partway through the heat spell, she said, one five-year-old staggered into class and began vomiting uncontrollably. As the child stood in a puddle of watery bile speckled with half-digested chunks of lunch, Simangan felt herself panic. It was the worst moment she'd experienced in two decades of teaching, she said.Heat Storm Vera hit Tacloban particularly hard, tormenting the city for a total of more than nine months. Standing in a rare spot of shade at Sagkahan High School earlier this year, Cloe Novella, 17, recalled sitting in her class and trying to catch the weak breeze from one of the classroom's old fans when she realized one of her best friends hadn't said anything since they sat down. Turning around, Novella saw her friend appeared to be sleeping, tapped her, and quickly realized that her friend had lost consciousness. Novella's teacher told one of her classmates to fetch Polido, who came and carried the student to the clinic, where she recovered. She was one of more than 40 who Polido estimated fainted during Vera.The Philippines soon suspended in-person classes across the country and has since changed its school calendar to avoid exposing students to the most extreme temperatures. Yet for Novella and her fellow students, Heat Storm Vera kickstarted a new era of near-perpetual heat.LJ Corsanes, 17, said he frequently plunges into temperature-induced panic attacks. "It's like going into a fight," he said of going outside. "It's like opening a door to hell."Over the entire 1960s, heat storms hit Tacloban for only 7 days, and the city experienced 245 days of ordinary heat waves. This decade, ordinary heat waves have touched Tacloban for fewer than 40 days - but heat storms have engulfed the city for more than 1,470 days. That's over 200 days a year.Tropical archipelagos such as the Philippines are particularly vulnerable to heat storms, Reuters' analysis shows. The warm ocean heats the air from below while sunshine not only beats down from above but also reflects off the surrounding water. Other tropical islands, such as Guam, Haiti and much of Indonesia, spend most of the year in heat storms.The implacable heat is forcing students to learn grim new skills. In July, Polido gathered 80-odd teenagers for first aid training with the Red Cross. Over two days, they practiced how to begin chest compressions, how to lift an unconscious person to safety, and how to position someone who has passed out so they don't choke on their tongues.For some, the heat has become eerily normal. Novella said it makes her feel "like I am burning in pain and fire." But, she added, "It is not strange, because I am used to feeling the heat already."IVORY COAST, NOVEMBER 2023-JUNE 2024: DEATH OF A CHOCOLATE CHIEFIn his half-century as a farmer of cocoa, the raw ingredient of chocolate, Chief Brou Kouassi earned enough money to marry five times, send his 12 children to school, and float a little cash to his neighbors. He even had a nickname - "A Nous Deux", or "Just Between Us" - a phrase people used when they came seeking assistance on the hush-hush.In 2023, Heat Storm Vera started stalking Digrikro, the village in western Ivory Coast where Kouassi had been chief since 2000. At first, the heat storm came and went, lurking for up to two weeks at a time. Then, beginning November 1, Vera besieged the area for more than four months straight, sometimes sending temperatures above 38 C (100.4 F). "La secheresse" - the drought - also began in November, according to local farmers and United Nations rainfall data.His sons had taken over the hard labor, but every morning Kouassi still pulled on his boots and went out to survey his 22-hectare farm. As Heat Storm Vera shriveled the pods and sent brittle leaves falling from the branches, Kouassi would shake his head and lament that he had never seen so many trees dead or dying.His sons would go out in the morning with their machetes to cut down the cocoa pods but return just a few hours later because, as Kouassi's son Jules put it, "the trees didn't give us anything." Jules said the cocoa yield on his portion of the land for February to April 2024, an important harvesting time, was less than half of normal.Ivory Coast and its neighbor Ghana produce about 50% of the world's cocoa. But in the wake of Heat Storm Vera, the harvest in those two countries fell by half.Vera had collaborators, among them disease, which preys more easily on heat-and-drought-weakened cocoa trees, and an El Nino, which likely intensified the heat storm. But Vera and the drought it exacerbated were relentless, with the heat storm lingering over one cocoa region of Ghana for a total of almost 11 months. In 2024, the price of cocoa almost tripled.In West Africa, where almost all the cocoa is produced by smallholder farms such as Kouassi's, the stakes were existential. Kouassi urged his sons to abandon cocoa for heat-resistant crops such as rubber or cashews. "He kept saying, 'If you don't replace the cocoa trees, you'll have nothing to eat,'" recalled Jules.In June 2024, as Heat Storm Vera took its last licks at Digrikro, Kouassi fell ill. After a medicinal broth of leaves didn't work, his family sent him to the hospital, where Jules recalls doctors saying his father had malaria and anemia. He spent four days in the hospital, at a cost of 320,000 CFA, or about $525. But his illness persisted, so they sent him back again, paying another $525. They considered a third trip for the same high cost, but they couldn't afford to keep sending him back because the devastation of the cocoa crop had beggared the family.Kouassi's one-story concrete farmhouse offered little respite from the clammy heat. As his illness worsened - swelling that began in his feet spread all the way up to his thighs - he struggled to sleep more than a few hours each night. With money scarce and Western medicine failing, he asked to go to the village where he was born to visit a traditional healer or, if that failed, to be buried next to his parents.Kouassi traveled by bus, which typically takes more than six hours to cover the 200 kilometers, much of it on a choppy dirt road. Years earlier, before heat storms shattered his livelihood, Kouassi had built an eight-bedroom house there with a large patio, where he relished visits from relatives and neighbors, some whispering hush-hush stories. His sons hoped the more comfortable environment and traditional remedies might help him regain his health.The healer took 90,000 CFA, a little less than $160, then refused any more payments even though he kept bringing clay pots filled with medicinal concoctions. But his father continued to decline, Jules recalled, and finally pulled his son aside and asked him "to take care of the family because he didn't know if he would survive." Kouassi died on October 27, 2024, aged 68. No official cause of death was given.His beloved cocoa farm has not recovered. Many of the trees are dead or sick, Jules said, and revenue remains in a rut. Kouassi himself lies buried under a blank headstone, his family unable to afford the finishing tribute: a name plaque. Nor have they been able to raise enough money for a traditional funeral, a fact that torments Jules. In the culture of their Baoule ethnic group, the failure to hold that ceremony - complete with a sheep sacrifice, drumming and dancing - means his father cannot go peacefully into the afterlife. "It's like his soul is still walking around here," Jules said, "unable to rest."FEBRUARY, 2026: A MASSIVE NEW HEAT STORMOver its lifetime, Heat Storm Vera drifted over nearly 85% of the planet, more than any heat storm on record. Its peak size, covering 31.3% of the Earth on January 5, 2024, was also a record. Until this summer.Heat Storm Raimundo, which broiled Europe and stoked massive wildfires in Spain and France, extended over 33.8% of the globe on August 28. Since its inception on February 28, 2026, Raimundo has touched almost three quarters of the planet's surface.Both heat storms spent time over a melting Nepalese glacier before its collapse on August 26 and the catastrophic flooding that followed, killing thousands. Early indications suggest that warming temperatures contributed to the collapse of the glacier and the bedrock beneath it.Up until the glacier gave way, it had spent about 58% of this decade in a heat storm or heat wave, up from 7% during the 1960s. For the six days immediately preceding its collapse, the glacier had been blanketed by Heat Storm Raimundo.Raimundo isn't yet finished. It has been heating the earth for 235 days and counting.

items.title: PSG take on Barcelona in 2026 Champions League clash amid French protests
items.summary:
In a test for both teams and the strained French police, Paris Saint-Germain hosts Barcelona in a Champions League showcase against the backdrop of violent unrest across France.
PSG and Barcelona head the standings, though Liverpool or even surprising Stuttgart could end Tuesday on top of the table.
The game, which will need a robust security presence, takes place in a very different context to when PSG beat Manchester City 4-2 away last week.
What began in France as protests against school conditions has expanded to include a wide range of other groups and causes. There have been violent clashes, fires and looting.
An emergency meeting with top government officials on Monday confirmed PSG-Barcelona and other soccer games in European competitions can go ahead after the possibility of calling off games and other big events was discussed.
Liverpool could go top with a win over Villarreal if PSG and Barcelona draw, or on goal difference if Andoni Iraola's team can rout its Spanish ..

items.title: Hockey India opens doors to fans with free entry at Asian Champions Trophy
items.summary:
Hockey India on Tuesday announced that fans will get free entry to all the matches of the men's Asian Champions Trophy to be held in Jalandhar and Mohali from October 27 to November 5.

items.title: 9 injured in fire at 13-storey residential building in Mumbai's Kurla
items.summary:
A fire broke out in an electrical duct of a 13-storey residential building in Mumbai's Kurla area early Tuesday morning, leaving nine people, including three children, injured, civic officials said.
The blaze erupted around 6.53 am at Kohinoor HDIL Building No. 5 in Kurla West, where flames spread along electrical wiring and duct installations before fire brigade personnel brought it under control at 7.21 am, they said.
According to a civic official, eight residents suffered suffocation as thick smoke engulfed the structure, while one person sustained an injury to his right leg.
The injured, including a five-year-old boy, two teen girls and a senior citizen, were rushed to Rajawadi Hospital, where their condition is said to be stable, he said.
Personnel from the Mumbai Fire Brigade, police, power company, a 108 ambulance service and ward staff were mobilised for assistance, officials said.
The cause of the fire and extent of the damage are yet to be determined, they said.

items.title: Tiger Shroff case: 3 accused taken to Mumbai
items.summary: A Mumbai Police team departed Kota for Mumbai by car on Tuesday, carrying three individuals allegedly involved in the firing incident targeting actor Tiger Shroff.Subhash Chandra Mishra, Additional SP of Kota city, explained that the team halted in Kota overnight to avoid traveling after dark. "They were tired also due to the journey from Mumbai to Kota, so it was not safe for them to travel in the night," he stated, adding, "The Mumbai police team has now left for Mumbai with the accused by road."Ramswaroop, SHO of the Railway Colony Police Station where the suspects were held, noted that strict surveillance was maintained overnight. "Since the incident is very serious, security is being maintained as per the usual procedure. I was here throughout the night. The CCTV cameras are directly connected to the police headquarters," he reported.Local police apprehended the three suspects in a general compartment of the Pune–Jaipur Superfast Express at Kota Railway Station on Monday morning. Two of the detainees were identified as Ritik (alias Roshan) from Begusarai, Bihar, and Rehan from Sonipat, Haryana; the third is a juvenile.Also read: Shroff firing: Accused recce'd football ground for a monthFollowing their handover by Kota city police, Mumbai Police formally arrested the suspects and presented them before a magistrate, obtaining transit remand to transport them to Mumbai.Police investigations indicate that Rehan had been communicating with Anil Pandit, a suspected associate of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. The gang later claimed responsibility for the attack in an unverified social media post.The shooting occurred on Sunday evening in Mumbai's Juhu locality, where at least two men opened fire on Shroff's vehicle before fleeing on a motorcycle. Five to six rounds were fired at the vehicle; the actor escaped mostly uninjured, but his driver and a nearby bystander sustained injuries.Investigators recovered the motorcycle believed to have been used by the shooters abandoned in Andheri. The suspects had escaped to Surat before boarding a Jaipur-bound train, planning to proceed to Delhi by bus and eventually escape to Nepal.Mumbai Police have registered a case citing charges of attempted murder along with relevant sections of the Arms Act.

items.summary: Minamitane: Japan launched an uncrewed spacecraft toward the Martian moon Phobos on Tuesday on a mission intended to become the first to collect samples from the small rocky body and return them to Earth for analysis.The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Martian Moons eXploration spacecraft lifted off aboard an H3 rocket before dawn from the Tanegashima Space Center in southwestern Japan.The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars in August 2027 and return samples to Earth in 2031. JAXA hopes the mission will shed light on the origin of the two moons of Mars and deepen the understanding of our solar system's early stages.Phobos, the larger of the two Martian moons, orbits the planet three times a day. Phobos has an irregular shape with dimensions of about 27 km by 22 km by 18 km (17 miles by 14 miles by 11 miles), and orbits roughly 6,000 km (3,700 miles) above the Martian surface.JAXA aims to collect at least 10 grammes of material from its surface and return it to Earth for analysis.The launch marked the first interplanetary mission for Japan's H3 rocket. The country's flagship launcher experienced a high-profile failure on its inaugural flight in 2023 when its second-stage engine failed to ignite, but has since completed a series of mostly successful launches.

CJI inaugurates Ladakh bench of JK HC
items.summary: Leh: In a historic milestone for the administration of justice in the Union Territory of Ladakh, Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, on Sunday, inaugurated the newly established Ladakh Bench of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at Melongthang, Leh.The establishment of the Bench marks a significant step towards bringing justice closer to the people of Ladakh, particularly those residing in remote and far-flung areas, by reducing the hardships, time and expenditure involved in travelling to Srinagar or Jammu for judicial proceedings.Also read: Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Kargil chief to seek dissolution, likely to join BJPThe dais was graced by CJI Surya Kant; Justice M M Sundresh, Justice P S Narasimha and Justice Arun Palli, Judges of the Supreme Court of India; R Venkataramani, Attorney General of India; Vinai Kumar Saxena, Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh; Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma and Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Judges of the High Court; and Ashish Kumar Kundra, Chief Secretary, Union Territory of Ladakh.The occasion was further graced by Justice Tashi Rabstan, former Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh; all the Judges of the High Court, accompanied by their spouses; the Director General of Police, Law Secretary, Administrative Secretaries and senior officers of the army, civil administration, police and other departments of the Union Territory of Ladakh.Officers of the High Court Registry, headed by MK Sharma, Registrar General, Additional Solicitors General of India (ASGIs), Deputy Solicitors General of India (DSGIs) and Presidents of the Bar Associations of Leh and Kargil also attended the ceremony.Upon his arrival, the CJI was accorded a ceremonial Guard of Honour, following which he unveiled the inauguration plaque. A group photograph was taken, followed by a guided tour of the Court Complex. The formal proceedings commenced with the National Song and National Anthem, followed by a welcome address by Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.In his address, Bhati emphasised that access to justice had been the guiding principle behind the establishment of the Ladakh Bench. He observed that, under the visionary leadership of the CJI, the establishment of a constitutional Court in one of the highest-altitude regions of the world marked a historic milestone in bringing justice closer to the people, particularly those residing in remote and geographically challenging areas of Ladakh.The CJI also virtually inaugurated the Green Wall, symbolising the judiciary's commitment to environmental conservation. The initiative was marked by the presentation of planters to the dignitaries and screening of a short video. In his special address, Vinai Kumar Saxena, Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh, termed the establishment of the Ladakh Bench a historic milestone in strengthening access to justice in the region. He also highlighted the significance of the Green Wall initiative in promoting environmental conservation and ecological sustainability in Ladakh.Justice MM Sundresh, Justice P S Narasimha and Justice Arun Palli, Judges of the Supreme Court of India, and R Venkataramani, Attorney General of India, also addressed the gathering on the occasion.A major highlight of the ceremony was the launch of four significant initiatives by the Chief Justice of India, comprising the Green Wall and digital initiatives, namely, the e-Filing Portal and Document Management System (DMS) for the Ladakh Bench and the Online Recruitment Portal of the High Court.The e-Filing Portal will enable advocates and litigants, particularly those from remote areas, to file cases electronically without travelling to the Court, while the DMS will facilitate digital management of judicial records. The Online Recruitment Portal will streamline recruitment in the High Court and District Judiciary, promoting transparency, accessibility and efficiency.Significantly, the Ladakh Bench shall function as a fully IT-enabled, paperless Court, equipped with modern digital infrastructure. The Court Complex also houses a dedicated Digitisation Centre, Filing Counter, Bar Room, Litigants' Sitting Area, Conference Room and Video Conferencing (VC) Room, ensuring efficient and technology-driven judicial functioning.The CJI Surya Kant also initiated work for the installation of solar power systems at 11 locations, reinforcing the judiciary's commitment to renewable energy and sustainable infrastructure.Also read: Ladakh integral to India, China's denial can't change facts: MEAIn his Presidential address, the CJI emphasised the role of technology and legal aid in ensuring access to justice in Ladakh and appreciated the e-Initiatives launched to overcome geographical barriers.The programme concluded with a vote of thanks by Ashish Kundra, Chief Secretary, Union Territory of Ladakh, followed by the National Song and National Anthem.The inauguration of the Ladakh Bench, together with the launch of digital and infrastructure initiatives, heralds a new chapter in the judicial history of Ladakh, reaffirming the judiciary's commitment to accessible, efficient, technology-enabled and citizen-centric justice, while ensuring that geographical distances and difficult terrain do not become barriers to the administration of justice.

items.title: UN food agency cuts aid to Palestinians in Gaza, West Bank amid fund crunch
items.summary:
The United Nations has cut food assistance to 5,00,000 Palestinians in Gaza and 2,00,000 in the West Bank due to a serious funding shortage, the head of the UN food agency said.
Carl Skau, acting head of the World Food Program, on Monday urged the international community to provide USD 450 million so the agency could restore the cut assistance and provide hot meals and food parcels in Gaza and the West Bank for the next six months.
Because of the money shortage, the number of people receiving assistance was reduced this month from 1.6 million to 1.1 million in Gaza and from 4,00,000 to 2,00,000 in the West Bank, he said.
Skau, who had just visited both territories, told UN correspondents in a video briefing from Jerusalem that life in Gaza remains "absolutely brutal" and incredibly dangerous, with UN teams recording about 50 attacks per day in the past week.
Nonetheless, he said that since last October's ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, "we have been able to push back on famine"

items.title: From France to Albania, social unrest sets Europe's streets ablaze
items.summary:
Rising fuel costs, discontent with the state of schools, declining public services and a housing crisis have created perfectly stormy weather for an autumn of protests in Europe.
Crowds have taken to the streets for weeks in major cities, resulting in arrests, looting, injuries, and violence across France, Italy and Albania. In Spain and Portugal, tent camps have sprung up in protests against unattainable rents and housing costs.
Young people "feel disappointed with the (social) model and experience a strong sense of uncertainty and a lack of control," said Maria Silvestre, professor of sociology at the University of Deusto in Spain. "And when specific situations come together, a spark suddenly ignites that is capable of channelling that discontent and driving people into the streets."

items.title: Big news for Maharajah INR Bond investors
items.summary: The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) said in a notification issued on October 19 that it has exempted interest payments on rupee-denominated bonds issued by the New Development Bank from tax deduction at source for eligible investors.According to the notification, the exemption applies to holders of Maharajah INR Bonds who are Indian residents or foreign institutional investors, for the 2026-27 tax year and subsequent tax years.A Maharajah bond is an onshore, rupee-denominated bond issued within India. It is issued and settled in rupee (INR) rather than in foreign currencies.This bond is sold inside India's domestic markets to both local and foreign institutional investors. This makes it different from Masala bonds, which are issued outside India -- in global markets.The New Development Bank (NDB), established in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa (BRICS), is a multilateral lender that finances development projects in emerging markets and developing countries (EMDCs).NDB's rupee bond programme is intended to strengthen India's domestic capital markets and enable the bank to fund projects in local currency, thereby limiting exchange-rate risks for borrowers, the bank's website notes.Also read | Global investors against use of judicial anti-avoidance rule by tax officialsAccording to an ET report published in August 2026, the NDB plans to invest $7.5 billion in India over five years. The BRICS-backed lender aims to expand local-currency financing, offering emerging economies alternatives to funding denominated in dollars.The bank is drawing up its General Strategy for 2027-2031, which will define its lending priorities and the allocation of funds among countries.

items.title: FSSAI issues notice to Zepto over complaint of delivering expired besan
items.summary:
Food regulator FSSAI has issued a notice to e-commerce firm Zepto for the alleged delivery of expired besan (gram flour) to a customer.
In a social media post on Monday, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said it has issued a notice to Zepto Marketplace Pvt Ltd regarding a complaint about the delivery of expired besan.
"A complaint on social media platform X alleged delivery of two packs of Besan past their use-by date. Both packs reportedly carried the marking "USE BY: 12-09-2026" ( September 12), indicating they were expired at the time of delivery," the regulator said.
FSSAI has directed Zepto to verify the complaint and submit order, delivery, warehouse, seller and product details.
"The company must explain the root cause of the delivery and confirm withdrawal of affected stock, customer notification, refunds and corrective measures to prevent recurrence," the regulator said.
FSSAI has also asked Zepto to submit a written response.

items.title: ACME Solar signs 300 MW power supply pact with Seci at ₹6 per unit
items.summary:
ACME Solar Holdings Ltd on Monday said that through its subsidiary, ACME Greentech Twenty Pvt Ltd, it has signed a Power Procurement Agreement with Solar Energy Corporation of India (SECI) for 300 MW / 1,200 MWh assured peak supply.
The assured peak supply under SECI's FDRE-IX tranche was at a tariff of Rs 6 per unit, with an effective date of October 6, 2026, a company statement said.
This Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) project supports the growing need for reliable, dispatchable clean power during evening and night-time peak demand, helping strengthen grid stability as renewable energy's share of India's power mix increases, the statement added.
Following this agreement, ACME Solar's under-construction PPA-signed contracted portfolio stands at 4,310 MW out of total under construction contracted capacity of 5,380 MW, it stated.
Through this FDRE project, ACME Solar will supply 4 MWh per MW of contracted capacity for any four hours daily during the non-solar hours, .

The government has asked Meta, owner of Instagram and Facebook, to ensure that its recommendation systems do not result in "disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to step up checks on content that could cause public disorder or incite violence or other unlawful activity.
The advisory by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), dated October 10, asked Meta to undertake appropriate measures to provide adequate context in relation to photographs, videos, graphics, or other content depicting ongoing public events, particularly where the authenticity, date, location or circumstances of such content may not be readily apparent to users.
Although the advisory does not identify any specific incident that prompted its issuance, it comes amid protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and opposition parties in Delhi demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over the Special Intensive Revision ..

"The three suspects have been detained by Kota city police today at Kota station," the official told PTI.
Three unidentified assailants opened fire at Shroff's car in Mumbai's Juhu area on Sunday evening. The actor escaped unhurt, while his driver and another person were injured.
The Lawrence Bishnoi gang has claimed responsibility for the attack, according to a viral social media post, but police have yet to verify its authenticity.

items.title: Agha hits fourth ODI ton as Pakistan defeat Sri Lanka in tri-series opener
items.summary:
Salman Ali Agha made a triumphant return to the Pakistan team with his fourth ODI century in a 37-run victory over Sri Lanka in the cricket tri-series opener on Sunday.
Agha hit 107 off 90 balls and Pakistan scored 305 all out in 49.5 overs after Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis won his fourth successive toss and chose to field.
Agha was among seven Pakistan cricketers summoned back home at the end of August during a tumultuous tour of England after Agha had led the team in the first test.
Pakistan pace bowlers overcame heavy dew and threatening half centuries from Pavan Rathnayake (79) and Janith Liyanage (60) to dismiss Sri Lanka for 268 in 48.1 overs.
Captain Shaheen Afridi picked up 3-55 while Naseem Shah pinned down Sri Lanka's top-order with impressive swing bowling to finish with 2-43. Haris Rauf ran through the tail with 2-48 while seam all-rounder Faheem Ashraf grabbed 2-49, including the key wicket of Rathnayake.

Australia won the toss and opted to bowl. Play began after a nearly two-hour delay with South Africa's openers taking the hosts to 11-0 in 5.3 overs at lunch.
Rain further delayed play after the break before pacer Scott Boland struck twice for Australia. He bowled Aiden Markram for 11 in the ninth over. Next ball, David Bedingham was caught behind for a golden duck, leaving South Africa at 12-2 in 8.5 overs.
Tea was taken when rain returned shortly afterward, but there was no further play on the day with the threat of more rain on Monday.

items.title: PSG suffer Nuno Mendes injury blow ahead of Champions League clash
items.summary:
Paris Saint-Germain left back Nuno Mendes faces several weeks out after suffering a tear in his left thigh, the French champion said Sunday.
The Portugal international came off in the 53rd minute of Saturday's 3-1 win at Strasbourg in Ligue 1.
The injury is also a blow for PSG coach Luis Enrique, given that Mendes would likely have marked Barcelona superstar Lamine Yamal in their Champions League game on Tuesday.
Yamal operates from the right flank and often cuts inside. The 19-year-old Yamal has scored nine goals overall this season for Barcelona, which has won all its 11 games so far in La Liga and Champions League, and has also been in terrific form for Spain.
Veteran France left back Lucas Digne will likely start the game at Parc des Princes in Paris.

items.title: Hellmann takes over as Eintracht Frankfurt CEO after Krosche steps down

Eintracht Frankfurt has appointed former board spokesman Axel Hellmann as its CEO.
The German club said Hellmann will also take on the role of board member for sport on an interim basis following the departure of Markus Krosche at his "own request."
"With his appointment as CEO, the supervisory board is counting on continuity while, at the same time, strengthening the leadership structure at the top of the club," Eintracht Frankfurt said.
Hellmann has worked for Eintracht Frankfurt since 2001 in various functions, playing a pivotal role in the strategic, financial and organizational development of the club over 25 years, the club said.
The supervisory board earlier Sunday granted Krosche request to step down from his role with immediate effect. Krosche had asked Mathias Beck, chairman of the supervisory board, "to relieve him of his duties as board member for sport with immediate effect," the club said.
